headline: OSHA: mineral spirits vapor in industrial washer caused Brent Industries blast — both victims identified, investigation continues
paragraphs: Two employees died and two to three others suffered minor injuries when a series of explosions tore through Brent Industries, an industrial dry-cleaning and laundry recycling facility at approximately 2900 South Avenue in south Toledo, at approximately 4:50 a.m. on August 18, 2026, during a shift change. One victim was identified as Mary Allen, 64, of Toledo; a second adult male victim was also confirmed. Brent Industries processes shop towels, gloves, and absorbent pads using solvents and mineral spirits — materials that contributed to the intensity of the blaze. The building suffered partial roof and wall collapse; a three-alarm fire response drew multiple departments to the scene. WTOL, 13abc, Spectrum News 1, NBC News, and ABC News all reported the fatalities on August 18.

The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration confirmed it is investigating and has determined the cause: flammable vapor from mineral spirits — a petroleum solvent used in the facility's industrial washing machines — ignited. The Lucas County Coroner's Office identified the second victim on August 19 as Heladio Garcia Perez, 46; both Allen and Perez died of blunt force trauma, the coroner said. Family, friends, and coworkers gathered on South Avenue for a vigil for Mary Allen on the evening of August 19. OSHA noted it has six months to complete its investigation before releasing findings. Investigators from cleveland19.com reported the probe was still in progress 36 hours after the initial blast.

Brent Industries has a documented history of serious industrial incidents and regulatory violations: OSHA cited the company's Toledo plant in 2004 for two serious violations — including failure to protect workers from death or serious injury from a 207-degree steam release — and the company's Alabama facility experienced a similar explosion and fire in 2015 that killed one worker. The Toledo plant uses tanks of mineral spirits in its textile reconditioning process for work gloves, shop towels, and industrial rags. OSHA's investigation is expected to examine whether adequate safeguards for flammable-vapor hazards were in place.

Toledo City Council members Theresa Gadus, John Hobbs III, and Nick Komives held a press conference at the Brent Industries site on South Avenue on August 27, 2026, drawing renewed political attention to the aftermath of the August 18 blast that killed Mary Allen and Heladio Garcia Perez. Surveillance video showing the moment of the explosion also surfaced in the August 25–27 reporting window, per local outlets. The council members' presence at the scene nine days after the explosion signals that political pressure on city and regulatory response is escalating; Brent Industries was discussed at the August 25 Toledo City Council session alongside the Flock camera situation, per The Blade. The OSHA investigation remains open with no findings expected for months under the agency's standard six-month investigation window.

The U.S. EPA released on September 1, 2026 a list of chemicals present at the Brent Industries facility at the time of the August 18 explosion, disclosing that the site held stoddard solvent and sulfuric acid, the latter contained within forklift and scissor lift batteries. EPA stated it has not detected any dangerous levels of chemicals in the air. Brent Industries has hired a contractor to conduct daily air quality monitoring during regular business hours. 13abc reported September 2 that residents who live near the South Avenue facility are voicing health concerns about whether chemicals from the explosion could affect them in the long term; residents called for independent testing and greater company transparency about all hazardous materials on site. A World Socialist Web Site report on September 3 — two weeks after the blast — documented families and community members demanding accountability.

13abc published a records investigation on September 4, 2026 revealing that the Brent Industries facility on South Avenue had experienced six fires between 2021 and the August 18 blast — the first on January 14, 2021, when a large dryer overheated while gloves were being dried. Toledo Fire & Rescue conducted an inspection of the facility on May 7, 2025 and found five violations, including insufficient records of inspections, testing, and maintenance of exit and emergency lighting equipment, and issues with a sprinkler system valve requiring replacement. There is no available public confirmation that a follow-up inspection was conducted or that the violations were corrected before the August 18 explosion. The facilities' documented pattern — six fires, unresolved 2025 safety violations, and OSHA's 2004 citation for failing to protect workers from a 207-degree steam release — is now part of the public record as the six-month OSHA investigation proceeds.
why_it_matters: A fatal industrial explosion at a solvent-processing facility in south Toledo is relevant to the region's manufacturing safety environment and workforce. Two workers killed at a shift-change incident raises immediate questions about industrial safety compliance and emergency response that OSHA and local regulators will need to address. South Toledo's industrial corridor is part of the broader economic geography that Toledo's site selectors and workforce development programs are counting on; incidents of this scale draw regulatory attention to the area and may affect the operating environment for neighboring facilities. The national coverage (NBC News, ABC News) brings outside attention to Toledo's industrial base during a period when the region is actively marketing manufacturing readiness.
